subtopic: SUGGESTED ALL-CANADIAN FAIR    REJECTION OF INVITATION BY MONTREAL

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUGGESTED ALL-CANADIAN FAIR    REJECTION OF INVITATION BY MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the house the government did all that was within its power to persuade the group meeting in Paris in recent days to select Montreal as the site for the 1967 world's fair.
When the hon. member asks me why Canada did not adopt the same tactics that were adopted by a totalitarian country, I can only say that Canada pursued proper tactics, and has not always open to it the kind of methods that are open to a totalitarian government. We proceed by the methods that are open to a democratic government. I assure the house that every effort was made properly to persuade that meeting to choose Montreal as the site for the 1967 world's fair.
The house is aware of the fact that the matter was resolved only after five votes were taken, and the contest was exceedingly close. Austria withdrew several days ago and the issue then became a straight question of choosing Moscow or Montreal. On the first two ballots a two thirds majority was required. The result of the first ballot was 17 for Moscow and 13 for Montreal, and on the second ballot 16 for Moscow and 14 for Montreal. On the remaining ballots a clear

majority only was required. The result of the third and fourth ballots was a tie, 15 votes for each side. On the fifth ballot one country changed its vote, and the result was determined in consequence by a vote of 16 for Moscow against 14 for Montreal.
We regret the result but, Mr. Speaker, I wish to leave no doubt in the mind of any hon. member that everything that could properly be done to persuade the group meeting yesterday to select Montreal as the site for the 1967 world fair was done and efficiently done by the two ministers who represented Canada at the meeting.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: SUGGESTED ALL-CANADIAN FAIR    REJECTION OF INVITATION BY MONTREAL
speechtext: In view of developments of recent weeks which bear on the position taken yesterday, did the government at any time, without adopting totalitarian methods, suggest to any of its friends that there were advantages in joining this bureau? The answer is no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUGGESTED ALL-CANADIAN FAIR    REJECTION OF INVITATION BY MONTREAL
speechtext: I do not think it would be appropriate to launch into a detailed review here of what might or might not have been done in relation to any particular country. There were 30 countries represented at this meeting and, as hon. members are aware, certain countries, associated with the Soviet philosophically, had recently joined the group. So far as Canada is concerned, we acted at all times in a straightforward way. We do not profess to be able to control the decisions of other countries. Canada, I think it is our proud boast, does not exercise sway over any satellite countries.

speechtext: I have a question for the Minister of Public Works. speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. member for St. John's East for giving me notice of the question. In reply may I say that I have had the opportunity to read the newspaper report relating to the statement made by Premier J. R. Smallwood in the Newfoundland house of assembly on Monday, May 2. Premier Smallwood stated:
The government of Newfoundland has not appointed St. John's as their agent for the proposed land assembly project and the government of Newfoundland have no authority to appoint the city as their agent.
On March 10, 1959, more than a year ago, the province of Newfoundland requested of the dominion government, through its deputy minister of municipal affairs, that the possibility of a land assembly project be investigated with a view to entering into an agreement with the city of St. John's as an agent of the province under section 36 of

the National Housing Act. Since this type of arrangement has been used in many other provinces, the federal government was prepared to work with the city of St. John's as an agent of the province.
In accordance with this request the federal government agreed to investigate the proposed project with the city of St. John's. This investigation has now been under way for two months. When the province completes its delegation of authority to the municipality and when the investigation is completed, the formal agreements can then be drawn up if the project is approved by the federal-provincial partners. Surely no more evidence is required that the federal government is prepared to participate in federal-provincial housing projects in Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, while I have the floor I might reply to the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday with regard to Elliot Lake, and outline what the government is doing in that respect.
The problems concerning the Elliot Lake community have been receiving continued and intensive study by the government. Based on the information supplied by various organizations representing Elliot Lake and on investigations conducted on the spot by representatives of the government, plans have been made to examine every aspect of the situation at Elliot Lake with a view to assisting in sustaining the community.
As I mentioned earlier in the house, the problem requires action on a broad front. The community itself is showing commendable effort. The mining companies are engaged in searching for other industries for the area. The government of Ontario over the years has shown a very active interest in the development of the community and is concerting provincial measures to aid in the continued well being of the community. The dominion government also has an interest in the welfare of Elliot Lake.
To further these purposes a committee has been appointed with instructions to consult with the appropriate representatives of the government of Ontario, the mining companies and the community of Elliot Lake. The committee has also been empowered to examine the possibility and feasibility of any projects under federal government jurisdiction that might be considered for location in the Elliot Lake area.
At the present time several proposals Involving industrial establishments are being considered. In addition, the Department of National Defence has been making inquiries as to the practicability of establishing a training centre at Elliot Lake. The continuance of as much employment as possible under the circumstances is a major concern,

and all factors affecting employment are being reviewed with the mining companies.
Pending the outcome of the consultations and investigations now going on it is not possible to state precisely the type of assistance that may be given to the Elliot Lake area. The committee is actively engaged in attempting to find an acceptable solution to the problem.
Hon. Mr. Macaulay, minister of energy resources in Ontario, has informed me that similar activities are being undertaken by a committee appointed by the government of Ontario, and in conversation with him we have arranged to have a meeting of the two committees at the earliest opportunity.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister if it is not the case, judging from his answer, that the federal program of assistance for Elliot Lake at this time is merely a further examination by the appointment of a committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that is an unnecessary gloss on the statement I have made. The Minister of National Defence reported to the house just the other day that his department is very actively engaged in assessing the possibility and feasibility of locating a defence training establishment at Elliot Lake. This is going ahead, but a decision cannot be reached overnight or within a few days because of the obligations involved. If this is gone ahead with it will be a very substantial contribution by the dominion government to a very active and important community.

Mr. Chairman, when I adjourned the debate last Friday I was pointing out that the Minister of Agriculture, in his second speech, made certain accusations concerning the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska. He accused the hon. member of having delivered in this house a purely political speech on agriculture.

There is another reason why the minister should have accused the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska of having made a political speech in this house, and it is this. The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska reminded the minister and the Prime Minister of their solemn pledges to the Canadian people in the field of agriculture. Mr. Chairman, I do, however, wish to support the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm on one point. He pleaded with the farmers to join the U.C.C. This, 1 think, was shrewd advice on his part, and I earnestly support his suggestion.
In the report of the Stewart commission which was set up by this government-a most creditable move, in my opinion-it was indicated that the U.C.C. and the co-operatives -probably mostly the co-operatives, as they are more particularly concerned with the economy-had helped narrow the spread between production costs and consumer prices, a problem which was investigated by the Stewart commission.
On the subject of price spreads, I should like, Mr. Chairman, to say a few words about that royal commission. I think the government acted very responsibly in setting it up. I shall indicate later what I think of the commission's recommendations and especially of the attitude adopted by the government later on.
When the Prime Minister announced the creation of that commission in the house on December 10, 1957, he said, as shown on page 2123 of Hansard:
The chairman will be Dr. Andrew Stewart oi Edmonton, president of the University of Alberta, formerly lecturer in agricultural economics at the University of Manitoba and dean of business affairs at the University of Alberta. The other members of the commission will be Mrs. W. R. Walton Jr., of Toronto, a member of the board of directors of the Canadian Association of Consumers since its inception in 1947; Dr. W. M. Drummond of Bristol, Quebec, and Guelph, Ontario, head of the department of agricultural economics of the Ontario Agricultural College; Mr. Howard Mac-Kichan of Halifax, Mr. Romeo Martin of Montreal, Mr. Bernard Couvrette of Montreal and Mr. Cleve Kidd of Toronto.
The commission is appointed under part I of the Inquiries Act, their powers being to inquire into the extent and the causes of the spread between the prices received by producers of food products of agricultural and fisheries origin and the prices paid by consumers therefor; to determine whether or not such price spreads in general or in particular are fair and reasonable or are excessive, in relation to the services rendered; to make such recommendations as they deem appropriate if any such price spreads are found to be excessive, and to examine the adequacy of price information currently available.
I mention the personnel, sir, to indicate the high standard of those who have undertaken, at personal sacrifice, to discharge the important responsibilities which will fall on them.

Mr. Chairman, I am far from being an advocate of unmitigated socialism. I am not for government interference in all fields of human activity, and I am convinced that the system we have in America is still the best in the world.
However, the fact that we do not want out-and-out socialism is no reason why we should remain blind to the weaknesses of our system.
I believe the best way to avoid extremes is to have the intelligence to see our weaknesses and, above all, the courage to apply a remedy.
I have just pointed out to the house a weakness that I think we should try to correct.

It is precisely because of cases such as those that some of our people want the government to interfere in all fields. But I think that the government should take into serious consideration the recommendation of the royal commission on price spreads of food products and establish a permanent board on prices, productivity and incomes.
Even if the permanent board did nothing more than prevent similar abuses, I think we would have made a great step towards avoiding government interference in all spheres of human activity.
The government must take action respecting such shameless abuses.
What is the good of fine speeches, of talk about human freedom, if we lack the courage to correct the few weaknesses in our system.
The C.C.F. party has made a great many suggestions in the field of agriculture. I admit that several of them were most interesting and appropriate; the same can be said of other fields of human endeavour in our country. But, on the whole, the party's platform seems to give the impression that if the C.C.F. got into power, we would be living in an earthly paradise.
What I don't like about them is that they try to give the Canadian public the impression that if they ever occupy the treasury benches, it will mean the end of all the evils that plague mankind.
It will never be.

The C.C.F. platform is marvellous, even fascinating to me, but I believe it has come 2,000 years too late. Had it been made known before the fall of Adam and Eve, it would have been a benefit indeed.
I should like to say a few words now about dairy production, especially in Quebec. My colleagues are aware that Quebec produces more than a third of all the milk consumed in Canada.
Canadian farmers derive nearly 40 per cent of all their income from that industry, and for a great many of them, dairying represents 80 per cent of their total income.
It is therefore an important sector of Canadian agriculture, but particularly in the province I represent here with my other Quebec colleagues.
The situation has become critical, for the simple reason that the market is increasing from day to day, and that we have no support price on milk powder.

Sixty two per cent of the milk powder produced in Canada comes from the province of Quebec.
You will all remember that, in February 1960, milk powder was selling at 12 cents a pound. Today, it is down to 7J or 8 cents.
Canada produces about 170 million pounds of milk powder a year.
We consume about 120 million pounds, so that we have a surplus of a little over 50 million pounds. Now unless the price is supported, there is unfortunately a strong possibility that this milk powder will sell below production costs.
Farm organizations have submitted briefs and demands to the government on this matter. Some organizations have urged and are still urging the government to buy, if not all the surplus, at least between 35 and 40 million pounds of our milk powder surplus. Those associations have suggested a price of 10 cents a pound. This would have the effect of maintaining prices and stabilizing production to some extent.
There is no doubt that the government could also find markets. It is true, admittedly-I want to be candid about this-that this might cost the government about $2J million or $2 million, or even $3 million, but this surplus might well be given away to the Colombo plan as assistance to certain countries that need it. I think it would be a highly humane measure which would please the countries obtaining this help, though perhaps it would also cause some of my Quebec colleagues to grumble.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to speak on the agriculture estimates before the committee at the present time. Since I am a member for a constituency in Saskatchewan, namely Humboldt-Melfort, I feel it is my duty to speak on matters pertaining to agriculture. Also, I

would like to take this opportunity to say a few words, since I have just returned from a five-day Canada-United States interparliamentary conference which was held in Washington, D.C.
I must say I received some useful and interesting information on agriculture. We met with our counterparts from the United States Senate and House of Representatives, and discussed problems closely concerned with agriculture. We had a considerably detailed discussion on surplus wheat problems confronting both the United States and Canada. As you are probably aware, Mr. Chairman, Canada and the United States together produce about 20 per cent or 25 per cent of the world production of wheat.
In this connection, in our agricultural industry we have problems in Canada and in the United States which we can call common problems, and one of them is the wheat surplus. Wheat production in Canada and the United States in the past two years has exceeded the domestic consumption plus exports. Because of this there has been an accumulation of huge surpluses. Moreover, wheat surpluses are more likely to be of a long term rather than of a short term nature.
An expression used by a United States congressman was very disturbing to me. He said in no uncertain terms that at the end of this year the United States will be faced with a huge surplus of wheat, and they will likely have to adopt a more liberal approach to the disposal of wheat surpluses. Further, he said that by the end of this year the United States will have about a billion or a billion and a half bushels of surplus wheat on their hands. All this pointed up to a stepped up program, a program that has been ruinous in a way to us in Canada in the past. I refer to the give-away program, the Carter deal, and so on.
In this connection I might say that a few years ago the present government made some strong representations to the United States government and asked them not to dispose of their surplus wheat in our commercial markets. To the remarks of the congressman from Florida I expressed some concern, and pointed out to him that although we are not in a position to suggest methods by which they should dispose of their surplus, we hoped they would not do it in our commercial markets. I also emphasized the point that export wheat means much more to Canada than it does to the United States, because 60 per cent of their wheat production is consumed domestically while Canada consumes

only about 25 per cent of her production. Naturally we have to find markets for many more bushels of wheat in our country.
Another comparison can be drawn in this way. Wheat accounts for 20 per cent of cash income from all our farm marketings, while in the United States it accounts for only about 6 per cent. I also brought to the attention of the committee the need for a free world food bank. If we set up such a bank we would be in a position to achieve two purposes; first, to dispose of our wheat surplus and, second, to feed the underdeveloped peoples of the world.
After a two-day session the members of our committee passed a resolution stressing continuous, close consultation in order to avoid damage to other countries' commercial markets. In this connection I should like to say that wheat surpluses in the United States are large but that country, as I have already stated, can resort to give-aways and other methods to dispose of them. We in Canada cannot resort to these methods. The only avenue left to us is to take acreage out of wheat production and thus reduce our surpluses.
There are not many methods by which we can do this. We can put more acreage into edible oilseed production such as soya beans, sunflower seed, rapeseed, and safflower seed. The production of soya beans is restricted by climatic condition and in the western provinces, where most of the wheat is produced, we cannot go into soya bean production.
We have such production in Essex county.

It is very nice to hear the hon. member say that they have it in Essex county. I will deal with soya beans a little later.
The farmers of my constituency are not only good farmers but they are also pioneers in this new industry, the production of rapeseed. They were the earliest producers of rapeseed on a commercial basis in western Canada, and have done a magnificent job in establishing this western grain. When I see statements in the press and hear statements over radio and television that rapeseed will become a major crop in the future or that it is a new crop to watch or that here is an opportunity for a new crop, then I must say that I sense my responsibility to these western farmers and feel it is my duty to speak in the house on behalf of the rapeseed producers. I am doing this in the full knowledge that this new industry is not getting the attention it deserves.

By this I do not mean to say that we in the west are looking for subsidies, deficiency payments or other financial assistance. Far from it. All we are looking for is an opportunity for the rapeseed growers equal to that enjoyed by other grain producers in the west. I know that hon. members have heard me speak on rapeseed quite often and that I have almost become a laughingstock. Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that this is not a laughing matter for the western producers. They are aware that they have to take acreage out of the production of wheat, and the only method the farmers of the three western provinces can resort to is to plant rapeseed.
At the beginning of the industry the freight rate structure was the biggest factor in preventing the industry from developing. Over a period of 10 years freight rates were allowed to go up 125 per cent. The rate on rapeseed went as high as 80 cents per hundredweight, while on other grains coming under the Crowsnest pass agreement the rate remained at only 22 to 23J cents per hundredweight. This situation almost wiped out the rapeseed industry in 1959, and I have statistics here in that regard. In 1958 production in the three prairie provinces amounted to
626,000	acres, while in 1959 it had dropped to 218,000 acres, a drop to almost one third the acreage. Naturally the freight rate structure was a big factor in this drop, and it has also prevented the expansion of this new industry. The situation is very disturbing because we have just been able to introduce rapeseed oil and have it accepted by the edible oil trade. This was a very important decision. There is no reason in the world why carloads of oil could not be sold to the edible oil trade if the rapeseed growers were given proper attention.
The biggest single factor against the use of this oil in Canada is the fact that Canadian crushers are allowed to crush United States soya beans in Canada and thereby by-pass the 20 per cent tariff now in effect on soybean oil. Take note, Mr. Chairman, that there is a 20 per cent tariff on soybean oil but no tariff at all on imported soya beans. Here is what is happening in the crushing industry. On soybean oil imported for edible use there is a 20 per cent tariff while soybeans are allowed entry duty free. In any other type of manufacturing in Canada a tariff is charged on the imported material that goes into the manufacturing. A rebate on that tariff is made to the manufacturer when he exports his goods, but there is no rebate on that part of his production of manufactured goods that

Supply-Agriculture
is used in Canada. In addition, the manufacturer in Canada who exports to the British commonwealth must use 25 per cent of Canadian product in order that he may export to British commonwealth countries.
This is what is happening in Canada. The Canadian crusher purchases all the Canadian soybeans. He does not use any of those beans for crushing into oil for Canadian consumption. He uses those beans to make up the 25 per cent of Canadian material in the oil and meal that he markets in Great Britain and other favoured nation treaty countries. The soybean oil that he sells in Canada is made almost entirely from United States beans which come in free of duty, and the great bulk of the meal sold in Canada also is made from United States beans that enter duty free. In this way he entirely by-passes the 20 per cent tariff on soybean oil.
If our country is anxious to have a crop of rapeseed grown in western Canada we should immediately take action to see that any United States soya beans used to make oil sold in Canada should pay the 20 per cent tariff. If this were done it would mean that the growers of rapeseed, sunflower seed and safflower seed in Canada would be able to market their products at a little better price than they are getting now, but so far as rapeseed is concerned it would not raise the cost of the finished product by 1 cent. It would only bring the price of rapeseed oil up to the present price of soybean oil in eastern Canada, whereas now we have to sell it at a discount of about 2 cents per pound. One pound of rapeseed oil is equivalent to one pound of soybean oil. If this were done we could depend on a very large crop of rapeseed in western Canada with a reasonable price to the farmer, and at the same time take thousands and thousands of acres out of the production of wheat. I am afraid that if nothing is done the price of rapeseed this year will have to go so low that the industry will be practically wiped out.
Cottonseed oil, peanut oil and corn oil all enter Canada duty free, while on the other hand Canadian rapeseed sold in the United States must pay 1 cent per pound import tax. Since repeseed only sells for about 4 cents a pound, a 1 cent a pound import tax means a great deal to the rapeseed producer. Canadian rapeseed meal entering the United States must pay a duty of $6 per ton while United States soybean meal is allowed to enter Canada duty free.
To illustrate my grievance, I should like to point out that margarine production in

Canada in 1959 amounted to 152 million pounds. Preliminary reports show that in the production of margarine the following oils and fats were used: Soybean oil, 76.1 million pounds; cottonseed oil, 9 million pounds; cocoanut oil, 5| million pounds; palm oil, 10J million pounds; marine oils, whatever they are, 12.8 million pounds; animal fats, 4.7 million pounds, and other vegetable oils, 4.3 million pounds. Dr. B. M. Craig, a national research council scientist at Saskatoon and a very good friend of mine-he comes from my constituency-has made the statement that only one tenth of the margarine made in Canada is made from oilseeds grown in this country. Most margarine is made from these oils which I have just listed and which all come duty free into Canada from the United States.
As you can see, Mr. Chairman, under these adverse tariff and freight rate conditions the rapeseed industry cannot compete successfully against the cheap American soybeans that are brought into Canada duty free. This situation will eventually wipe out the whole rapeseed industry. Indeed that would be a tragedy for our agricultural industry, since rapeseed can play a very important part in our Canadian economy.
The remarkable change with respect to Canada's place in the world's rapeseed market and the important position which rapeseed may have in the years ahead calls for a good deal of attention to be paid to this valuable oilseed crop. Since 1958 rapeseed has been officially designated an edible oil in Canada. This new step opens up interesting possibilities for the use of rapeseed as a major ingredient in margarine and shortening instead of bringing in United States soybeans and oil duty free. Only a partial shift in this respect would require the planting of several thousand acres to supply the domestic market alone. Quite apart from edible use, however, it has been found that the industrial potentialities of rapeseed are very promising, particularly with respect to the blending of certain special lubricating oils and the production of grease. Everyday use of grease containing rapeseed oil has yielded top results. I should like to make here a statement that I read not so long ago in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix in regard to rapeseed grease that is used now on farm and other vehicles:
The first carload of a new grease using homegrown rapeseed instead of imported castor oil arrived at federated co-operatives Regina branch April 19.
Shipments of the grease are already on the way out to co-operative retail outlets served by FCL...
It requires 25 pounds of rapeseed yielding 8-10 pounds of oil to each 100 pounds of grease.

This is indeed a good discovery, and it opens up the use of rapeseed oil in this country. But equally as great possibilities are open for the farmer who produces rapeseed for the export market. The initial development of the rapeseed industry in the prairie provinces in recent years has come largely as a result of the demand of the export market. The largest part of the 1959 crop of rape-seed has been exported to Japan, which is our good customer for agricultural products. Here I should like to give you some statistics from the dominion bureau of statistics. It is stated that our best customer is Italy. Last year we exported to Italy about 100 million pounds of rapeseed oil or rapeseed. The second best customer is Japan, which bought about 81 million pounds of rapeseed; and our third best customer is the Netherlands, which bought 31,620,000 pounds.
During these last three years we lost some good and big customers. For instance, there was Belgium. In 1956 we exported to Belgium about 27 million pounds of rapeseed, and last year only about 1 million pounds. The same thing applies to Switzerland and so on and so forth. However, over the years we increased our export markets from a mere 60 million pounds to 225 million pounds in 1959, indeed a remarkable figure.
Reports that French interests are negotiating for the purchase of a considerable quantity of Canadian rapeseed have heightened Canadian hopes that a somewhat better market might be developed in Europe in the immediate future. A $5 million sale of rapeseed to the French government has been reported in Canadian grain circles. As I say, Canada has emerged from the position of a net importer of rapeseed in 1954 to that of the world's leading exporter, with exports of over 225 million pounds.
Rapeseed could become a major crop in the prairie provinces within the very near future if given the right attention. Oilseed production offers a partial solution to our surplus wheat in the long range view. It is possible that another million acres or one and a half million acres of rapeseed could be produced in the prairie provinces, taking into consideration the domestic consumption and export. This action would mean reducing the wheat surplus by 30 million or 40 million bushels a year, and at the same time it would bring cash money into the pockets of the farmers who go into the production of this edible oilseed. It would also mean a saving of millions of dollars to the Canadian treasury, since there would be much less grain for which storage would be required.

In conclusion I should like to stress again the importance of this crop by means of which it would be possible for our farmers in the west, particularly in Saskatchewan- since Saskatchewan may be called the wheat province of Canada-to take out acreages that would produce wheat and utilize them in producing this edible oilseed.

In the discussion of these estimates I am sure we regret- certainly we on this side of the house do- the inadequate statement made by the minister when he introduced his estimates, I think some time about March 1. His six minute speech on that occasion could hardly be regarded-
Your leader said it was a 15 minute speech.

-as the kind of speech that should be made by a minister administering a department in which some $113 millian are proposed for expenditure; and certainly it was not the kind of speech that one would expect from my good friend the genial Minister of Agriculture in respect of an industry that has reached in this country-as it has, I admit, elsewhere- a very critical stage.
The minister ought, at the earliest opportunity, to face frankly the critical situation that confronts farmers from one end of Canada to the other. I am sure the situation in my own county demonstrates the position in this particular, one to be found from one end of Canada to another. There the farmers are concerned not only about importations from the United States, as we have just learned from the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Rapp); they are concerned about the reduction-for instance, in the case of the tomato growers-of the acreage normally given them by companies such as the Heinz company and others. They are concerned about the closing down of canneries. They are concerned about the inadequate floor prices on some of the commodities under the agricultural prices stabilization act. They are concerned about the failure of the administration to include certain other products under the stabilization act. They are concerned, too, about the indications that the government is bit by bit abandoning or straying away from its original policy of floor prices under the stabilization act and resorting to a system of deficiency payments, as was characterized

Supp ly-A griculture
by its policy announced some months ago with such disastrous results in the case of hogs and eggs.
In my particular area, if I may be local for a moment, the farmers are also concerned about the price they will receive for Ontario grown wheat. The 1960 support price looks to be about $1.36 per bushel f.o.b. truck. The wheat producers board will want the stabilization board, I think, to increase the support price to a more realistic level, which I suggest should not be less than $1.60; that is at harvest to the producer. Not less than that should be done if the minister is going to be able to live up to the general kind of assurances which were given to the farmers in my area, as in other parts of Canada, by such statements as that of the Prime Minister when he said "We will assure the farmer of his fair share of the national income by maintaining a flexible"-and I underline the word flexible-"price support program to ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers based on a fair price-cost relationship."
To date the stabilization board price has not been of any real value to the Ontario wheat producers; I doubt that the minister would quarrel with this statement. One of these days the minister will be receiving representatives from the Ontario wheat producers, and I will be surprised if they do not ask for an exemption from the mandatory list of grains covered under the act so far as wheat is concerned. The reason for that is that they feel that 80 per cent of the ten-year average seriously affects their chances of getting a better price on the basis of negotiations with the trade. In any event this is a very important matter to farmers in Ontario, in my section of the country, and I hope this further plea to the minister will bring the action which he failed to take last year.
I hope also the minister will be able to indicate today when we may expect a decision as to the floor price on sugar beets. I would be interested in knowing whether the stabilization board has been able to take into account the losses which have attended the sugar beet growers as a result of the award recently made by the arbitrator under the contract between the sugar beet growers in southwestern Ontario and the sugar company at Chatham. The farmers as a result of that award have lost a considerable source of income, and it would seem to me, as the minister did indicate in reply to a question of mine, that in the fixing of the price this year that loss ought to be taken into account.
I would hope also that the minister and the board would take into account the different interests that prevail as between the

various sugar beet producing regions of Canada. The return to the sugar beet grower in western Canada last year may have been satisfactory to the sugar beet grower in western Canada but in that part of the country on whose behalf I speak at this moment, there was and is less satisfaction. Instead of having a general price it ought to be possible to have a price which will take into account the interests and concerns of the various regions. Therefore I hope the minister can tell us something about the government's intentions with regard to sugar beets.
I listened with interest to the speech which has just been delivered by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort. Soybeans, of course, are a very important product in my county and in the neighbouring county of Kent, in the province of Ontario. I have before me a brief which was prepared by the Ontario wheat producers' maketing board, the Ontario soya bean growers' marketing board and the Ontario grain corn producers' association. At page 9 of that brief I note the following:
The federal deficiency payment program is not designed to bring producers a satisfactory return for their product.
The wheat board's establishment of floor prices above the government support price exemplified the possibilities of maintaining satisfactory prices through collective action. Even in a year of surplus production as in 1958, no deficiency payment was necessary.
Soybeans were classified for support price purposes at the request of the soybean board who administered the records and made the distribution of the deficiency payments. Even with the deficiency payment from the federal treasury, growers maintain that price levels are below cost of production plus a fair margin of profit.
The soybean grower in my section of the country is not satisfied with the floor price of soybeans. It was $2.10 a year ago and is $2 now. The principle of averaging the price is such that the declared floor price is not the price which is received by a great many of the farmers. In any event, I can say to the minister that I attended a meeting recently in Tilbury at which farmers from the counties of Kent and Essex were present, and to which all members of parliament of all political parties were invited, where it was declared by this group that they were not satisfied with the price support on soybeans.
The hon. member who has just spoken was right and justified in drawing attention as he did to the importance of soybeans. Soybeans are the major domestic source of edible oils in Canada. The production last year, most of it in southwestern Ontario, totalled
6,649,000	bushels. This was equivalent to the production of about 70 million pounds of edible oil. To make up the deficiency in the

supply of edible oils, last year, to carry further the argument of the hon. member who has just spoken, Canada imported from the United States 10,900,000 bushels of soybeans valued at $23,400,000 and 23,500,000 pounds of refined soybean oil worth $3 million. So anything that could be done to meet the situation confronting the soybean growers I think would be not only in their interests but in the interests of such people as the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort, thus indicating the national character of some of these problems in agriculture.
I complained a moment ago about the speech of the minister. I said, and I say again now, that it was not the speech of a minister who fully appreciates the gravity of the situation confronting Canadian agriculture. The minister said nothing about the long range programs of which he, the Prime Minister and others spoke during the time they were asking the people of Canada to give them the opportunity to carry on government in this country. The minister said nothing about the reduction in net farm income in this country; he overlooked the point made by the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska that there was a decrease of 7 per cent in the net national farm income in Canada. That 7 per cent represents a serious diminution in the income return of the Canadian agricultural community, and I am going to suggest to the minister that the reduction is in fact greater than 7 per cent. I suggest to him that a careful analysis of the revised figures will show that it is over 10 per cent.

I wonder if the hon. member would allow a question. Has the hon. member taken into account the fact that in 1958 the net income of farmers was up by 20 per cent; that the 7 per cent reduction from 1958 is a 7 per cent reduction on an extremely high rise, and that the net income in 1959 is still more than 12 per cent higher than it was in 1957 when the hon. gentleman was a distinguished member of the government of that day?

The minister
did not ask me a question; he made a speech, and I welcome that, because I think a good discussion is very valuable. I take it you will note, Mr. Speaker, that the minister made a speech and that his remarks will not interfere with the time allotted to me.
All I can say to the minister is this. This statement of his is not new. The fact is that there has been a serious loss of income suffered by Canadian farmers notwithstanding the assurance given by the minister last year, and I say that instead of the actual drop being 7 per cent, careful analysis of the
Supply-Agriculture
figures will show that it is over 10 per cent. This is not at all consistent with the assurance given by the Prime Minister on April 25, 1957 or the assurance given by the Minister of Agriculture to the farmers of Canada that they would share more equitably in the national income as a result of the price support program which the present government was going to bring in to ensure adequate parity for agricultural producers. That is the point, and I do not think I need resort to many proofs to indicate that what I am saying is felt by farmers generally throughout Canada.
We have the speech on agriculture made by the Prime Minister on March 4, in which he outlined the general principles guiding government policy since he took office. The right hon. gentleman made six points, and he went on to say to the farmers of the west that they would not get the deficiency payments they were asking for but that the government was concerned about doing something satisfactory for western agriculture.
The Minister of Agriculture himself spoke differently. A report appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of March 18, 1960, as follows:
Hon. Douglas Harkness, federal agriculture minister, said Thursday he won't present any alternative to the proposed deficiency payment program on wheat, oats, and barley which was turned down by the federal cabinet.
He says he expects to be asked for an alternative, but he will tell farmers the matter is one for the entire cabinet, and it hasn't been decided yet.
Of course it is a matter for the whole cabinet. The minister says he expects to be asked for an alternative. Surely the government does not need to wait to be asked. It is the responsibility of this government to provide solutions for these situations. The farmers of Canada have put forward suggestions; they have made repeated representations to this government. They wanted to meet the Prime Minister and his government over the Easter recess to discuss some of these alternative plans.
When is this government going to meet the farmers, who are dissatisfied over the lack of action by the government on the request for deficiency payments on the three grains? When is this government going to indicate its willingness to sit down with the farmers to discuss this question? Is the government to have a meeting with these western representatives next week, the week after, or when? Is the government going to give satisfaction with an acreage assistance plan? Or is the situation this, that the government is merely waiting for the farmers themselves

Supply-Agriculture
to present alternatives? It is no wonder that the Union Farmer in its issue of April, 1960 said:
What the Prime Minister failed to mention was that no measures had been taken to actually increase farm net income by increasing the cash returns for the products farmers sell.
If Canadian farmers are to get "their fair share of the national income" as they were promised by Mr. Diefenbaker before and since he took office, it will have to be done in the same manner industry has been and is being assisted by subsidized prices.
Unless this is done, and done soon, the family farm will disappear, and Canadian farmers will end up as hired men in an industrialized agriculture operated by big business which will then pressure government into giving it protected prices.
The Prime Minister, in the speech to which I have already referred, went on to say:
With reference to the other matters to which I had intended to direct my attention, I will do so at the very first opportunity which comes to me during discussion of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
We all understand why the Prime Minister cannot do that at the present time; he is preoccupied with affairs outside the country. The fact is that we are not being given, either by the head of the government or by the minister responsible, any indication as to what the government intends to do with regard to the representations made by the western farmers in the face of the government's decision not to accede to the proposal for deficiency payments.
Then we have the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who interests himself in these matters. He was giving an indication to the farmers that if they put forward an agreed assistance plan it might receive the favourable attention of the government.

speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

May I ask the hon. member a question? He has my sympathy when he is speaking on agriculture and I did not want to interrupt him; but at one stage of his speech he mentioned something about the farmers in his particular area receiving $1.36 for their wheat today. Does he realize

Supply-Agriculture
that the farmers of western Canada are receiving possibly $1.23 today? If the hon. member requests this government to consider paying his farmers $1.60 a bushel, is he really sincere in this because if he is it is no wonder that there are no Liberal members west of the great lakes?

My hon. friend wants to know whether I am sincere and I certainly am. The two situations are not comparable at all. The hon. member is now saying that the price received by one group of farmers in one section of the country must necessarily govern situations that are not comparable in other parts of the country. For instance, the sugar beet farmers of western Canada received a better price for their product than the sugar beet farmers of central Canada; but that in itself is not necessarily an indication that the other position is wrong.
I am speaking about wheat.

My hon. friend is speaking about wheat. He is asking me whether I am sincere. I say to him that when the Ontario wheat producers come to see the minister in the month of May I will be greatly surprised if, in the light of their problem of negotiation with the trade, they do not ask for something along the lines of what I have suggested. The hon. member must recognize this; the plight of the farmer is serious not only in western Canada but in other parts of Canada, and that is why we have supported western Canada-
Answer my question.
-those of us who live in eastern Canada. I would expect the hon. gentleman to rise in his place and support the eastern farmer as well. His problems-
The hon. member has not answered my question.
My hon. friend has asked me to answer his question. I have answered his question but he does not like the reply-
The hon. member has not answered it.
-any more. I am sure, than will the Minister of Agriculture.
Will he answer my question? Why should the eastern farmer receive 40 cents a bushel more than the western farmer?
I have answered your question.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the last statement of the hon. member for Essex East who, as we all know, is a gentleman farmer. I wish to assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I have followed his career with a great deal of interest for a great many years. I am certainly satisfied that he is and always will be a gentleman but as one who has all his life been engaged in the agricultural industry I have very great doubts that he will ever be a farmer.
A champion of of the farmer.

I have listened to his remarks today, and they painted a very general picture when they touched on the sore point of agriculture. Certainly, he represents that fine county of Essex where I was born.
I do appreciate the problems of agriculture and the seriousness of the situation with respect to certain commodities that he outlined. I should like to help him in one respect. However, I should like to point out -and I am sure he would wish me to do this-that he overlooked in his discourse today the problem of the burley tobacco growers. This is a crop which is very important in his county and one which faces not only lower prices in 1960 but the problem that the marketing board and the tobacco growers are advocating absolutely no production of burley tobacco whatsoever.
I will admit that that is so.

There is no doubt in anyone's mind that the agricultural industry today faces a very real crisis, and we have heard in the house many representations to the effect that in the past 20 years the agricultural industry has been facing a revolution.
First of all, I should like to deal with the basic changes that this revolution is bringing about; second, I should like to deal with what farmers are doing in the face of those changing conditions; and, third, I should like to recommend what we as a governing body and the government of Canada might attempt to do to aid this serious problem.
Perhaps, for a little background, I might say that after world war II, a time when the major agricultural commodities were operating under ceiling prices, it soon became apparent that there would be scarcities all over the world in all types of manufactured and primary produce. It was evident that all over the world there would be a terrific demand for goods and services, including all agricultural products, and the future

looked very bright indeed. But it soon became very apparent to those of us engaged in agriculture that there were other factors at work over which the industry had very little control that would soon place the industry in an almost untenable position.
One of the major factors that caused this change was labour. This is not to be taken in any way as censure of labour or labourers but merely as pointing out what has actually happened. With the terrific demand that developed for consumer goods, naturally there was a great upsurge in industrial expansion to meet this demand, and since we did have a great industrial expansion in this country it soon became apparent that there would be a terrific demand for workers. Since the demand was so great it naturally caused wage rates to rise to a phenomenal degree, and it soon became quite evident to the agricultural industry that it would not be in any position to compete with other industries for its proper share of the labour which is so necessary in the economic production of agricultural products. Since there was this terrific competition and the agricultural industry had to pay more for wages, the cost of production of all agricultural products increased to such a degree that we soon became very much concerned about our ability to compete successfully in world markets.
Agriculture was hurt by labour and the high cost of labour in another way. Increased labour costs resulted in an increase in the cost of all the goods and services that the farmer must use in his business. Since both these factors had the direct result of increasing the cost of farm production, the farmer's costs did rise at a phenomenal rate.
There was one factor too that became apparent so far as labour was concerned. Labour soon became very selective in its desire for work. We in the riding of Kent find ourselves today in the peculiar position of being one region in Canada where, although there are thousands of people registered as unemployed in the country, we are unable to procure the necessary labour today for successful economic farm production. This situation was pointed up very seriously because at one period last summer, when there were literally hundreds registered as unemployed in the constituency of Kent (Ont.) it was absolutely impossible for a farmer to procure any of these registered unemployed regardless of the wage scale. When these workers were solicited to go out to the farms they never even put in an appearance, let alone make any inquiry as to the wages prevailing at that time. I should like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that at this time the farmers in my district were paying wages running from $18 to $25 per day.
Supp ly-A griculture
The consumers themselves have added to the problems of the agricultural industry because of their increasing demands with respect to the packaging, preparation, grading and freezing of farm commodities. Because we are primary producers, naturally all these extra costs follow the pipe line back so that for the most part they are tacked on to the cost of production of the farmer. By no means do we criticize consumers for their desire for quality and service. The fast pace of life today makes prepackaged goods almost a necessity for the housewife rather than a luxury.
These trends have had a direct result. They have placed farmers in the so-called cost-price squeeze. The farmer pays more for what he buys, receives less for what he sells and is faced with an ever-narrowing margin of profit. May I illustrate my point, Mr. Chairman? The selling price of soya beans has dropped since the war from a high of $3.85 to $4.25 a bushel down to the prevailing price today of $1.85 per bushel. That is the market price. Hon. members will understand that the government makes a deficiency payment to bring the price up to $2 a bushel. During this same period the cost of farm machinery necessary for the production of this crop has in the main doubled or even more, and the cost of farm labour has increased to a greater extent. This causes serious repercussions in the industry.
In my particular area we have a potentiality of almost twice the present production of soya beans. We have a potentiality of twice the production of sugar beets that we are growing at the present time. We could grow more canning crops. All these crops have a high dollar return per acre and with the economy under which we are working in our area, since we lie between industrial centres, we need this higher return per acre in order to operate successfully.
I am sure all hon. members are aware of the small margin of profit available to the farmer today. No one will dispute that as being a fact. That has been the basic reasoning behind all attempts to render financial assistance to this great industry. That is why we have increased the amount of farm loans, why the farm stabilization act was implemented, why we have price supports and the subsidization of prices.
I should like to deal for a moment with the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East about the stabilization act and his advocated price for soya beans. I should like to refer to the meeting at Tilbury which the

Supply-Agriculture
hon. member attended. As reported in the Chatham News, the hon. member is alleged
to have stated:
The higher price of $2.40 was certainly not unfair especially when the commodity is produced on a small scale.
Did the hon. member say $2.40?
Yes.
My hon. friend knows that cannot be right because the price is $2 now and was $2.10 last year.
I wish to assure the hon. member that in this quotation-
The hon. member is referring to the proposed price?
Yes.
Oh, I am sorry.
The hon. member supported the request for a price of $2.40 a bushel for soya beans.
That is right.

Although something like this seems on the face of it to be very justified and it is certainly not my intention to suggest to the farmers that they should take anything less for their commodity, may I point out that just across the border in the United States there is a surplus of over 60 million bushels of soya beans and the floor price there is $1.85. A stabilized price such as has been suggested by the hon. member would therefore cost the government 50 to 55 cents per bushel to subsidize this one industry alone, and I am sure that the taxpayers of this country would take a long look at such action on the part of the government. 1 point out, Mr. Chairman, that the farmers are not interested in a price of $2.40 or $2 or $2.80. What the farmers are interested in is their margin of profit between their costs and their selling price.
What is to be done and what can we do in these circumstances? I should like to point out that the farmers themselves are taking gigantic steps to meet the situation as it now exists. I resent it vehemently when any hon. member in this house or anywhere else portrays the farm industry as being down on its knees asking for a handout from government. I present the assertion that no industry in this world has been beset through history by so many major and continuing problems and has so successfully and valiantly fought back through the centuries.
What are the farmers doing? We have in this country today-and I am very thankful for it-in our agricultural schools, government departments and experimental farms

agricultural technicians who are providing second to none in the world today new varieties, new techniques, new fertilizers, new sprays and new farm machinery and have supplied a service to our industry without parallel in the history of this world. This is not by any means a political bouquet. It is on my part a sincere statement of fact.
Progressive farmers, taking advantage of these services and by the use of new mechanization and specialization, have changed their method of farming from growing six, eight or ten different agricultural products. They have changed their farming to one or two major endeavours and by the use of technical assistance and new machinery and by the time allowed for study and concentration have been able to produce today in Canada, in quantity and quality and at low cost, units to such a degree as would have been thought impossible even three years ago.
I have been on a farm where today I have seen two brothers feed 2,500 head of cattle in 20 minutes, something that would have been thought absolutely impossible ten years ago. I have been on farms where the milking parlours in which cattle have been milked are larger and contain more cattle than did the entire herd of these producers ten years ago. I have seen hogs produced by thousands on farm units. I do not mean commercial establishments; I mean farm units, units farm-owned, farm-operated and farm-managed. I have seen farmers joined together in co-operatives work in harmony in an endeavour by quantity purchases and quantity sales to widen the margin of profit. I have seen them join together in order to approach government and selling agencies with a few voices instead of the many which in too many instances confuse the issues of the day.
The farmer is trying. He is employing every bit of available agricultural and business science to cut his costs, increase his efficiency and make possible a living like that of his fellow man. This is what the farmer is doing. What can we do as a government?
There is no doubt in anyone's mind that the assistance given by this government has been enormous. I was greatly interested to hear the hon. member for Essex East speak about the sugar beet industry, a major portion of which is in my riding and about how bad he felt that the arbitrated prices were less this year than last year. I am certain we have no quarrel in that respect. However, it was our government which placed a floor price of $13 a ton under the sugar beet industry and made possible the retention of this industry of Canada which was in the throes of bankruptcy. I should like to point out to the hon. member that it was the

minister of agriculture of his party who, in visiting the sugar beet industry at that time, is alleged to have said that if they could not grow sugar beets at a profit, they should grow something else.
I think we must approach this agricultural problem on a much larger scale, with a much larger endeavour on the part of hon. members and government departments. Men who are engaged in agriculture are no longer satisfied with subsidies or with floor prices. The latter are at best a medicine to get this industry over a present ailment. They are not a feature that will get down to the basic facts troubling this great industry.
There are two things we can do. We can emphasize the experimental work being done to utilize farm products and to find a greater field of use for these products. We were fortunate enough to hear the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort discussing rapeseed this morning and speaking of the oil from this great grain crop being used as a lubricant. This is, in my opinion, one way in which we can expand here at home and abroad the use of our farm products, namely by concentrating on the development of new uses in this ever-changing world.
The other is the extension of world markets. I am sure we all agree that the selling of all products of Canada comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce. However, I should like to deal with what we in agriculture can do to help. The extension or world markets would take away the glut that has constantly hurt us in every aspect of agriculture. This is the old story: take a larger part of world markets. However, I should like to point out that possibly we are not doing it in the right way.
I have reason to believe that we have an opportunity of seizing on more world markets. I refer to the shining example of one man from my constituency making one trip to one country at one time and obtaining, mostly through his own efforts, the sale of nearly $1 million worth of farm products which are now in the process of being shipped out of this country from our constituency and from constituencies across Canada. I should like to point out that we have in our particular riding men in this day going across into the territory of the great neighbour to the south and selling to that country, which has the greatest surplus on earth, farm products, making a sale of farm products to that country. When we can do this, is shows that these markets are there. I think it is time that we developed salesmen in this country with the ability to sell farm products.

Is that Mr. Warwick?
Supply-Agriculture
Yes.

What does it mean to sell farm products? We have -a reputation for developing farm products second to none, such as wheat, dairy products, meat, sugar, white beans, and livestock. Anything you care to name in the way of agricultural products, we not only produce it but we produce it in high quality. We have in this country thousands of men who have a natural aptitude for salesmanship but who perhaps are not familiar with the aspects of our quality produce. I should like to point out that no longer is it the time perhaps to expect the men in our trade commissions and in our embassies overseas to recognize and to be able to sell successfully quality products of such a nature as those developed on farms today. These men, I point out, should be trained by our Department of Agriculture for this specific task alone and should be paid according to their abilities. If we want good salesmen let us pay good prices. Then with good training we can put them in various countries and then begin to move this great glut which we have today.
It is not impossible to sell in a market that is already crowded. I would like to point out that right in the United States, the greatest producer of automobiles today, it was possible for salesmen in Europe to come into the United States market in 1959 and sell 600,000 automobiles shipped in from Europe. That is the type of salesmanship that I wish to talk about today. This salesmanship is absolutely necessary and I am confident that we will have to come to it eventually.
In my riding today we have a burley tobacco that has been grown every year until this year. And what has happened? Due to lack of sales the growers association is recommending to the farmers that no burley tobacco be grown in their 1960 crop, resulting in the loss of millions of dollars to the farmers in my area. The sale of five, ten or fifteen million pounds of this commodity would have made all the difference in the world. Burley tobacco is not to be confused with flue-cured or cigarette tobacco. It is a heavier quality tobacco grown out of heavier soil and the curing and harvesting methods are far different. The tobacco I speak of is used principally in blends, in pipe tobacco and chewing tobacco.
We have the same thing in the sugar beet industry. Because of world conditions today and lack of sales, in the sugar beet industry in my area contracts are less than half of what they were in 1959. This is a deplorable situation but something we have to face. I

Supply-Agriculture
have every confidence that it we as a government seek to train men to sell a quality product such as we produce we can find the markets and surely the price would be far less than what the taxpayers of this country are being subjected to because of the countless subsidies and assistance given to the farming industry today.
Mr. Chairman, all too often our sales overseas go through the embassies of the United States and Great Britain. This is a necessity today because of world conditions. But is it preposterous to suggest that contracts which require agricultural produce should pass, not through the embassies of these two great countries but come direct to Canada.
We are an independent country. The world recognizes us for our diplomatic relations and the way we honour our obligations. Is it not time that we began to get a world reputation as traders, and would this not solve our basic problems? This will not be easy and we will meet with many failures. Perhaps today we have not the money to go out and do this on a world wide scale, but may I humbly suggest that if we are unable to do this, then let us take one particular section of the world, let us take one particular commodity of which we have too much, let us take and train men to go out into this district and let us see what we can do.
If we cannot sell there must be a reason. If we are too high in price, maybe we need some form of banking set-up to provide credit to those people who need it. If our quality is not up to that required by these other countries, we should know this because we have the men who can supply the necessary knowledge to provide the necessary quality. If we need different varieties we should find this out. It is only by digging into this problem in a major way that we can ever learn what is necessary for this great industry.
I think the time has come for us to start to plan and to use and develop agriculture as a major industry and a major business. It is time we started to employ business principles in this great industry to restore it to its rightful place among the Canadian industries of today.

Another farmer.
