Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to participate in this debate, but my remarks will not be prolonged. However, I do come from a rural riding and I am aware that there are problems in our agricultural communities but although promises

have been made that these problems would be solved they have not as yet been solved and the farmers are still waiting for the legislation which will be the cure-all of all these problems.
There is one aspect that I would like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture, and it is a paragraph to be found in a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture on April 13, 1960 having to do with dairy products. In my riding we have a considerable amount of dairy farming, and the paragraph in question reads as follows:
In addition, 25 cents per 100 pounds will continue to be paid for whole milk delivered for manufacturing purposes, exclusive of milk from producers who sell a portion of their milk in the fluid bottled milk market.
One would get the impression from reading this particular paragraph that if a farmer produced milk, a quantity of which was to be sold for the manufacture of either butter or cheese in addition to selling milk in the fluid bottled milk market, he would receive the 25 cents on the milk that was sent for manufacturing purposes but would not receive it for the bottled milk. But apparently in practice that is not the case. If a farmer sells one bottle of milk and the rest of his product is sent for manufacturing purposes, not only does he not receive 25 cents for that particular bottle of milk but he does not receive the 25 cents for the balance of the milk sent for manufacturing purposes.
Mr. Chairman, there are two points I would like to make here. First of all, I feel that the statement as made by the minister on April 13 is certainly open to confusion, because the way I read this particular statement, one gets the impression that 25 cents will be paid for all milk that is sent to the manufacturer for making into cheese and butter.
If you read it carefully I think not.

You can read it any way you like but you still get the impression that you do not get the 25 cents for bottled milk, but if you have milk which is sent for manufacturing purposes you will get the 25 cents.
As a matter of fact I have had a considerable number of complaints from farmers in my riding who have had to pay back the amount they received in subventions just because they happened to sell one or two bottles of milk to neighbours on either side. I think that is rather unfortunate, because this particular statement does lead to confusion. I also think it is very unjust that if one farmer or several farmers, as happens to be the case in my riding, should sell a very limited amount of milk in the bottled

milk market, then they are not allowed to have the subvention for the greater portion of their milk production. I certainly hope this matter will be cleared up by the minister.
First of all, I suggest the particular paragraph I have in mind should be rewritten so as to clarify the position once and for all. What is far more important still is that payments should be made to farmers in respect of all the milk that is sent for manufacturing purposes without discrimination against any who happen to sell bottled milk. It is my sincere hope that the minister will allow such farmers to benefit from this subvention. I am sure the purpose of this provision was to benefit the farmers, but by reason of this particular regulation any benefit which they may have been intended to receive from this legislation is being completely nullified.

In rising to speak at the beginning of the agriculture estimates, I think back to the estimates of 1958 and 1959. All of us who sit on the government benches can share some satisfaction in that regard. Any pride we take in the results of the accumulated actions arising out of these estimates should nevertheless be measured with a certain humility. Agriculture and those engaged in agriculture have been neglected during the greater part of this century, and the decline of the industry has been most noticeable and significant in the nation's mind during the past 14 or 15 years.
This situation has been one of the products of our ambition to become a great industrial nation. The neglect of the needs of agriculture and the lack of consideration given our agricultural resources, including the people engaged in that industry, in the years following world war I made the depression of the thirties much more severe for all Canadians. With the passage of the years of world war II Canadians began to talk of a new order that would emerge after the cease of that conflict. No one was more eloquent on that theme than the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. He made the memorable statement that if that new order was not well on the way before the cessation of hostilities we might well look for it in vain. His foresight in that regard mirrored the attitude and future of Liberalism in Canada. You can see where they are today.
The elections of 1949, 1953, 1957 and 1958 gave Canadians a good chance to assess the policies of all parties. The overwhelming results of the 1958 campaign were a tribute to the leadership of the present Prime Minister. But they were much more than that. In the hearts and minds of the Canadian people they were an endorsation of a national policy for Canada. After all, during the war Canadians were prepared to make sacrifices.
Supply-Agriculture
In the years immediately following Canadians, of necessity, saw the future of this nation drift at the whim of political expediency which saw narrow regional considerations dominate the decisions in our parliament. National policy as such was a stranger in the Canadian parliament.
Today I wish to look at these estimates, and the agricultural industry, and match them to the pressing needs of the Canadian nation. There are several ways of dealing with these estimates. It would appear from reading Hansard and the news and editorial pages of our influential newspapers that the yardstick generally used is cost to the treasury; cost to the taxpayer. There have been a few men who have used a different yardstick, a yardstick considerate of the needs of Canadians in other walks of life. If one follows their search to strengthen Canada's national policy he is compelled to acknowledge that for many years Canadians have neglected to utilize the agricultural economy in such a way as to strengthen and build the general economy of Canada along sound and balanced lines. This can be amply illustrated by a comparison of the population in agriculture, the measure of agricultural production and the share of the national wealth that those engaged in it receive. As long as Canadians allow this situation to continue our national economy will be subject to serious and severe problems in so far as attaining strong industrial communities and stable and improved employment patterns is concerned.
I know there is a widespread view that great nations are industrial nations. I believe most of us will agree that Canada has a great industrial potential. I think most of our people will agree that we have not reached that potential. Indeed, it could be estimated that it will take nearly a quarter of a century, perhaps longer, to realize our ambitions in that regard. The question that must be answered soon is what will happen in the meantime. There is no doubt this immediate period will have a tremendous effect on the lives of all Canadians for years to come.
Last fall I travelled in Ontario, in the province of Quebec, in New Brunswick, in Nova Scotia, in Manitoba and in Saskatchewan. Everywhere I went I found farm people asking the same questions. Everywhere I went I found conditions in rural areas very similar. I was shocked by the lack of attention and encouragement that the agricultural industry has suffered over a long period of years in these areas of Canada. I have reason to believe the same situation has prevailed in other parts of Canada as well. I can tell you, sir, and the members of this committee, that I was impressed with the area of application

Supply-Agriculture
where the new Farm Credit Corporation could well serve both a social and an economic purpose. The new crop insurance legislation is still to be demonstrated, but here again I saw a need of this legislation in all these provinces.
However, the measure of legislation that can be a most effective instrument to bolster the Canadian economy and eliminate some of its inequities is, of course, the farm stabilization act. If we read the act and its preamble, we see it was designed to stabilize farm income and ensure farm security. Nevertheless, it would seem to me that it has a much greater service to perform. It could very well be a cornerstone-one which has been overlooked too often in the past-upon which this nation can embrace some of those national economic problems which have remained with us for the greater part of this century. To read the farm stabilization act is to think in terms of a balanced agricultural economy. It brings to mind such terms as support prices, deficiency payments and other payments. I think it is fair to say that there has been some measure of disagreement as to the use to which each one of these can be best applied.
There appears to be a great deal of confusion in this regard. That has been so from the time this legislation was first mentioned as possible legislation. Farmers and farm organizations are expressing a confusion of opinion. Then there have been those who have urged the government to try this, that and anything-indeed to try nothing-and it seems to have been their hope that by some process of trial and error or even by default we might find a method that would prove reliable.
These considerations are inconsiderate of the immediate position of farm people and if followed for any period of time will throw the entire stabilization act and program into disrepute. That would be a calamity for the agricultural industry and for the Canadian nation.
It is my opinion that deficiency payments should be more properly called incentive payments and should be used only as an instrument to promote production. They should seldom be used in connection with a commodity in a surplus position unless this commodity commands a ready export market. These incentive payments used judiciously could have a far-reaching effect on the agricultural industry, on farm income and on Canada's trade and dollar balances. For those commodities in surplus position, support prices appear very desirable.
Farm organizations and farmers alike are on record that these support prices should

be set at non-incentive levels. The beauty of support prices is that they tend to uphold the entire price structure of a commodity and this is an important consideration in building a healthy agricultural community. It is equally important as an aid in balancing the Canadian economy. Flat payments which more properly might be called deficiency payments can be useful in levelling out those segments of the agricultural economy that cannot be reached successfully with incentive payments or support prices.
Net cost of the operations of the stabilization act for the year ending March 31, 1959 was $15,124,100 for all commodities. The net cost of all support price operations since 1946 has been only $100,073,260.26. The publicity and emphasis given the cost of the program for the period ending March 31, 1959 are to be wondered at. I remember the words of the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska which were disturbing to farmers and farm organizations. One was almost led to believe that it was unreasonable to expend this amount to support agricultural stability and security. Fifteen millions of dollars is less than one dollar per capita to ensure the food supplies of this nation. Looking at this amount in relation to the serious problems facing labour and industry I am inclined to believe that these national problems cannot and will not yield to better days until Canadians are prepared to invest three or four or even seven or eight times the $15 millions paid out under the stabilization act for the year ending March 31, 1959.
Yet there are those who still maintain the ideal situation would be an agricultural industry without these artificial aids. I will not labour you with a recital of the artificial props that have become so much a part of the entire economic and industrial structure of this country. Rather I would say, add to the estimates I have outlined the amounts that could be reasonably justified for the producers of grain in western Canada, who incidentally are producing a product that can be successfully merchandised in world markets, and it might bring the increased estimates to an amount that could be considered a decisive factor in meeting the needs of labour and industry. There are those who have a peanut mentality and they would no doubt still ask for greater action but I see some who have dissenting frowns.
I ask you, sir, to consider that other problem which has been receiving considerable discussion during the present session. Someone has estimated that it will cost the federal treasury millions through payments out of the unemployment insurance benefits fund. Surely this nation would be better served

by expending an amount to create a demand for goods and services needed in agricultural communities; a demand that would be shared right down the line through the local small businessman, the wholesaler, the distributor, the manufacturer, and all the way from the farmer on the remotest homestead right back to the industrial employees of the St. Lawrence river basin.
During wartime this nation found it expedient to put every shoulder to the wheel. Surely in peacetime we could be even more productive of the needs of Canadians for employment and the fruits of employment. This cannot and will not be done by allowing as important a segment of the Canadian population as those in agriculture to suffer only a fractional opportunity to meet their neighbours' needs in the industrial and labour fields of this nation.
The farm stabilization act can be a most effective instrument in the Canadian economy. Since 1946 legislation on the books has been used to make returns so disastrous as to chase enough people out of production of any commodity that may be reaching surplus proportions. Balance is thus swung to the other extreme, at the end of a trail strewn with the wrecked and shattered hopes of farm people. It is my belief that there is a better alternative. The use of incentive payments on commodities for which there is a demand and market will change production patterns without such disastrous and ruinous dislocation of individual farm enterprise. Moreover, it is of a more orderly nature and of value not only to the farmer but also to those who handle, warehouse, distribute and merchandise farm products. It can also be argued that incentive payments serve to reward those who are willing to risk investment where it can be used to strengthen and build the Canadian economy.
Then there is that most intriguing matter of defining or deciding just what constitutes surplus in so far as any given commodity is concerned. In the grain business with which I have lived all my life it is considered that Canada needs a carryover of anywhere from 300 to 450 millions of bushels of wheat to service our annual domestic and export markets. It is of course easier to carry grain than perishable products. Last year we had a good example in the dry skim milk market. At one time we were approaching panic. Not too much later our surplus supplies had been absorbed. When you consider that it required only about $8 million to protect the stability of the entire Canadian dairy industry for the greater part of the production in the board's hands from the years 1957-58 and
Supply-Agriculture
1958-59, it would be difficult indeed to say that we had any real or dangerous surplus of dairy products.
Another classic example is eggs. Those who were the most enthusiastic advocates of a program to discourage production must, I think, admit that by the time the new deficiency payment program was to start the market had absorbed all, or almost all of those supplies which had been considered surplus.
The prospect of fluctuating egg prices is not one that Canadian consumers would appreciate. These illustrations serve as evidence that the problems of surpluses, while considerable, are not nearly as great as some well informed people try to make out. The associated problems are intriguing and will no doubt be with us for many years. From time to time circumstances may not work out as well as they have so far, and the federal treasury may be called upon to finance sizeable surpluses of some commodities. This will be the exception to the rule if proper use were made of incentive payments and provided that floor prices were set at nonincentive levels. Of course, such a program would require the use of flat or deficiency payments, where required.
If Canada is to become the great industrial nation that her resources justify; if Canadians are to enjoy secure employment in the period leading to that objective, the reality of that objective can be enhanced and hastened by the acceptance of the role of agriculture and the farm stabilization legislation in particular as one of the protective valves in this intervening period that can cushion the needs of labour and industry, both of whom are suffering growing pains that in the years gone by were never cured by dismissing the possibilities that are in the application of sound national policies, recognizing the continued and increasing interdependence and prosperity of both labour and industry with that of agricultural people.
A little over two years ago, when this party came to power, it inherited a legacy of problems which had been shirked by the former administration. That was one of the reasons for the change of government. In almost every field of activity that affects farm people that administration ran headlong and recklessly to the destiny that is theirs today. They allowed freight rates to climb by 120 per cent without any active concern for the national railway problem which is of the utmost importance to people on the prairies and in the maritimes and to others in every part of Canada in every

Supply-Agriculture
industry, including agriculture. They allowed the freight rate problem, and that of general transportation, to mushroom into a monster, without any active concern as to its effect on the economy of this nation. The people of Canada are watching the present survey which has been authorized and are hoping that as a result of those deliberations, and above the confusion and chaos of the past many years, a national transportation policy may now evolve.
Those who produce grain in western Canada are vitally interested in this question, as are all who depend upon grain production for their livelihood. They expect the government of Canada to respect those long standing agreements which were instrumental in the building of settlements in western Canada and, incidentally, providing this nation with an item of major export significance. Wheat is one of the few commodities that has enjoyed the confidence of the export market over the years.
The economic prospects for Canada in the coming year have been encouraging. In every report that I have read no one has ventured to expect that agriculture will share fully in those economic expectations that have been forecast. Indeed, it can be shown with the use of statistics that farm costs have continued to rise in the face of declining farm income. It is true that there are fewer farmers than there were, but even this fact cannot camouflage the situation in which farm people find themselves, a situation which is calling for greatly increased capital outlay to compete successfully.
The Farm Credit Corporation will prove of benefit to many in this respect; but there are many who cannot qualify. They already have an investment at the present time. They have the experience in their chosen line, and are of an age where change of occupation is not easy, even if they were provided with training for new jobs. They find themselves embarrassed for lack of purchasing power for the very things that can be produced by Canadians in other walks of life who have been laid off their jobs for want of a market. This inequity of income under which the people in agriculture are suffering is an old story in Canada. It has always been the forerunner of rough weather for the rest of the economy.
The government is still comparatively young as governments are known. I should like to think that this government will distinguish itself in the years ahead as one which was ready to blaze new trails of security for all our people in every part of Canada.
In the short period that I have had an

opportunity to share with the rest of you this closer look at our national economy I have become prouder than ever to claim the name and occupation of farmer. It would seem to me that this industry, one of the most basic in this nation, stands ready, as it always has, with a contribution to the future of this nation worthy of much more consideration than it has received throughout the long period of years. I ask you all to take a closer look at what the people in agriculture have been able to accomplish despite the obstacles that have hampered their progress. I ask you all to consider what they could do for Canada if given a better opportunity.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to commend the Minister of Agriculture on his fortitude and his ability to withstand the pressure within and without. After all, this is a pretty tough time for any minister to handle agriculture. I should also like to thank him for the concessions that he has given and the understanding that we will get a few more.
The constituency that I represent is for the most part a progressive, mixed farming district. Supplemented as it is with the oil and forestry industries our problems are not as pronounced as many others. However, I would certainly be remiss in my duty if I did not point out that in common with many other parts of western Canada 1959 was probably one of the poorest years in our history.
While approximately 80 per cent of the crop was threshed last fall, threshing was completed under abnormal and expensive conditions and the grain, as hon. members know, was mostly tough and damp. Further the balance of the crop, which came through the winter much better than expected, has deteriorated considerably. Moreover, quite a section was badly damaged by hail. So in general the agricultural industry is not in too healthy a position.
A certain section of our farmers who are well established in mixed farming, who are engaged in dairying and the cattle industry, are doing comparatively well while on the other hand there are a number of other farmers who are not firmly established and as a consequence are experiencing a very difficult time. The main problem in agriculture, as I see it, stems from the surpluses of grain and the farmers' inability to find markets for wheat. I believe implicitly in the ability of the farmer to compete with the world if he has the market. He therefore finds himself in a very difficult position, right in the middle

of the price squeeze. In my humble opinion, Canadians as a whole must accept this situation.
I do not believe for one moment that we can subsidize farm products for export. On the other hand, I believe we must subsidize the products we consume at home. It is not reasonable to expect the farmer to produce products for our domestic use for less than production costs and a fair profit. This is not an easy problem, and most will agree that support prices tend to bring other problems. Be that as it may, I contend that the producer is entitled to a fair price for products consumed in Canada, and I would hope that the matter will eventually be resolved.
As is to be expected, I have had a number of submissions from local farm unions in support of acreage payments. I would therefore urge upon the government, at least until a fixed plan is adopted, that the acreage payment be reinstated. I think it can be said in all honesty after a brief examination of the numerous measures taken by the government to assist agriculture that the government has done a lot. The measures I speak of have been recorded on numerous occasions so it is not my intention at this time to go over them again. For my purposes I should like to discuss the Farm Credit Act.
In brief, this is a two-pronged affair, encompassing as it does (a) the replacement of the Canadian Farm Loan Act and, (b) part III, legislation for young farmers. With reference to (a), the Canadian Farm Loan Act, as hon. members know the ceiling was raised from $15,000 to $20,000 with amortization at 5 per cent interest over 30 years. This continues to serve a need for farmers who have a 50 per cent or better equity in their farms and who wish to convert or extend their operations. In passing, I would indicate that the one main criticism which prevails would be corrected and that the new management will see that a realistic approach is taken to land values as they exist today.
With regard to (b) or part III of the Farm Credit Act, this provides for loans up to $27,500 spread over 30 years at 5 per cent interest to farmers between the ages of 21 and 45. This is commonly known as the package deal and will in my opinion reach down to the source of a common problem. In other words, it will provide the funds to set up an efficient family farm unit and will permit the adjustment of production to favourable market trends.
Its success and impact on the agricultural industry will, of course, depend on its administration. Let me say that we are particularly fortunate to have Brigadier Rutherford as chairman of the corporation. Brigadier
S upp ly-A griculture
Rutherford is well known and has to a large degree been responsible for the publicly acknowledged success with respect to the rehabilitation of veterans on farms. Accordingly, with the integration of the farm credit legislation and the V.L.A. staff there will be 200 trained, experienced and dedicated resident advisers who are well employed throughout the agricultural areas of the country. I think it is most significant to observe that the corporation will provide a pre-counselling service as well as a postsupervisory service.
Both these services are paramount to the success of this forward and far-reaching legislation. To begin with, let us look at the pre-counselling service. What does this mean? It can, of course, mean much or little. For the moment let us visualize a credit adviser, with the aforementioned qualifications, calling on an applicant to assess his whole proposition, that is, the ability of the applicant as a farmer, his family, the production capacity of the farm and the stock and equipment. On the completion of this assessment I can imagine the credit adviser sitting down at the kitchen table with the farmer, his wife and family and as one of a team bringing out the factors for and against the proposition. In the first instance, if the proposition shows the potential for success the matter is comparatively simple. The credit adviser can in a diplomatic manner interject some new ideas into the farmer's plan of operations and recommend the loan. When the loan is approved, he will naturally follow up with the supervisory service required.
The big and most important factor is precounselling service where the proposition does not support a loan and, in some instances, it will even be found that the applicant and his wife will have to be told, in as kindly a manner as possible, to get into some other form of livelihood commensurate with their ability. I am sure that the credit adviser will be able to do this on the farm in a manner that will cause very little pain to all concerned.
The question is this: Do we stop there and leave the applicant and his family to their own resources? I must emphasize that this is not good enough. I would on the other hand, contemplate that this counselling service would be continued and if not by the credit adviser by someone else with the time to do so, one who is well versed in welfare work and with direct connections with industry. Yes, above all, it must be someone who is interested in citizenship to the extent that through his counselling and help the applicant and his family will be given a new start in life.

Supply-Agriculture
I have been discussing the production side of agriculture, a policy directed to the task of assisting a section of this industry in reorganizing itself into sound economical family farm units so that advantage may be taken of every technological and production line method which will reduce production costs and permit adjustment of production to fit more favourable market trends; and I would hope to follow up at a later date on the marketing side of this question.
In conclusion, I submit that we must as a government and as Canadians maintain our agriculture industry in as healthy a position as possible. Apart from the fact that we must eat, there is no better place to build character than on the farm. A child born on the farm starts out with something to do and he does it. As a consequence, he is self-reliant and is brought up more or less to stand on his own feet. Fortunately for our general economy, they do not all stay on the farm.

I should like to reply briefly to some of the speeches and remarks which have been made here today on the agriculture estimates. The hon. member for Lapointe and the hon. member for Essex East both complained that I did not make a longer speech in introducing these estimates. It came as an agreeable surprise to me to learn that the members of the opposition are so anxious to listen to my voice at length. I should like to point out to them, however, that on January 25, in the throne speech debate, I made a full length speech here in connection with agriculture and general agricultural policy. Again on February 23, which I would point out was just about ten days before the introduction of the agriculture estimates, I made another full length speech in reply to hon. members in the opposition who had introduced to the supply motion an amendment dealing with agriculture. In that connection I dealt with general agricultural policy and general agricultural questions. In view of these two long speeches already along this line, and as I am not one who likes to see endless and useless repetition, I did not think it was desirable to make another long speech of a general nature on agriculture at the time the estimates were introduced.
The hon. member for Lapointe came back to the point which members of the opposition have been so fond of quoting ever since the dominion bureau of statistics figures came out, namely that the net income of farmers dropped 7 per cent in 1959. As I have pointed out on several occasions, what they completely lose sight of is the fact that the net income of farmers in 1958 was up 20 per cent over that of 1957. Hence, when they say

that the net income of farmers in 1959 dropped 7 per cent, what they are in effect saying is that the net income of farmers in 1959 is still up over 12 per cent above the net income of farmers in 1957.
There is no doubt that the net income dropped by that amount, in spite of the fact that the gross income was up almost as high as it was in 1958 and was the third highest on record in Canadian history. However, I think we must keep some sense of proportion in regard to this matter. As I say, the members of the opposition should keep in mind the fact that farmers in Canada had a smaller drop in net income by very much than did the farmers across the line in the United States and farmers in most other parts of the world and that we in Canada managed to keep up prices and to keep up farm income to a greater extent than was done in most other parts of the world during a period in which agricultural products of all kinds have been in surplus supply and when prices were going down.
The hon. member for Lapointe went on to say that the minister should have said what long range program we have to improve the position of agriculture. Our long range program has been put before this house by myself, by the Prime Minister and by various other members time after time and I think it is well known to the hon. members of the house. I know it is well known to the farming population of this country. Certainly I do not think it is justifiable for me as minister or for other members to keep on repeating the same thing over and over again.
The hon. member went on to say that there was a serious situation in the dairy industry. I do not know of any serious situation in the dairy industry. Actually the dairy industry has been one of the better off industries as far as agriculture is concerned. The prices of dairy products in Canada are the highest in the world and they are highest by a very considerable degree as compared with those in most of the other dairying countries. The support price for butter in this country, for example, is 64 cents. In the United States it is 57 cents. On the London market at the present time butter is selling for 38 cents a pound. Just those two figures give some measure of the amount of support that Canadian dairy farmers are receiving and of the very high degree of success which the government has had in maintaining the price of dairy products. As I say, we have managed to maintain them at the highest levels of any country in the world and at levels about double the prices that prevail in most of the

other dairying countries. That is the serious situation as far as the dairy industry is concerned.
The hon. member for Lapointe went on to say that we should have a support price for dry skim milk and that the lack of this support was a very damaging thing to the dairy industry. I should like to point out to him that a good deal of the trouble which the dairy industry has been experiencing in the last two or three years arose out of the fact that the previous government-the Liberal government-put into effect a completely unrealistic high price for dry skim milk of 17 cents a pound just prior to the 1957 election for purely political purposes. As a result of that price they encouraged a great expansion in the dry skim milk making facilities in this country and a great expansion in dry skim milk manufacture, and thus created the difficulties as far as dry skim milk is concerned and many of the attendant difficulties as far as the whole dairy industry is concerned. In order to restore the dairy industry to health it has been necessary to get rid of this support price on dry skim milk. We have done that by reducing the price gradually and then Anally eliminating it some six months ago.
The hon. member went on to talk about the price spreads commission or the Stewart commission which he said-I think aided a bit by the hon. member for Essex East-was established under a Liberal government. The previous Liberal government had absolutely nothing to do with this price spreads commission, of course. I do not think they even thought of such a thing. That a price spreads commission or inquiry would be set up and carried on was one of the election promises which we made and which we promptly carried out after getting into office.
What are you going to do about it? That is the question.
We are going to take the appropriate action that has been recommended by the commission.
Are you going to follow the recommendations of the commission?

As far as possible, yes.
The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort made a very good speech on rapeseed production. This matter of diversiAcation of crops in western Canada is an extremely important one. I should like to compliment him on his speech and on the interest he has taken in this problem. I should like to point out also that over the past two and a half years I have been making efforts to increase the use of rapeseed in various ways in Canada,
Supply-Agriculture
particularly with regard to its use in the manufacture of margarine. I managed to persuade one of the margarine manufacturing companies in this country to set up a pilot plant in order to work out procedures and so on for the use of rapeseed in the making of margarine. I trust that in the years ahead a great deal more of the content of margarine manufactured in this country will be from rapeseed oil.
As far as the tariffs on soybeans and the other sources of edible oils are concerned, I was a little surprised to And the hon. member for Essex East apparently supporting the position taken by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort. I say this because he is one, together with some of the other hon. members along the Liberal front bench who belonged to the previous Liberal government, who should be answering that question, because the previous Liberal government contracted on behalf of Canada not to put any tariffs on soybeans and these other edible oils and bound Canada under the GATT agreements not to do so. Therefore we are in the position that we cannot put any tariffs on these soybeans coming in from the United States and on other edible oils coming into this country unless we give some corresponding advantage to the country concerned.
All I was asking for was a satisfactory Aoor price.
The hon. member for Essex East indicated he supported-
I want a satisfactory floor price and so do my farmers.
The hon. member evidently would like us to put on a very high support price and encourage more United States beans to come into this country as a result of that.

I did not say
that.

That is apparently what he wants. That is the situation as far as soybeans are concerned. I think Canada made a very bad bargain under the previous Liberal government as far as soybeans and other edible oils are concerned in that at the time they entered into the GATT agreements they did not ensure that there were tariffs on such products. But they did not do that and as a result we are bound at the present time, and in order to put a tariff on them we have to give some corresponding tariff advantage to the country concerned.
The hon. member for Essex East, as usual in his speeches in this house during this session, attempted to paint a general picture

Supp ly-A griculture
of gloom. If one could take all that the hon. member for Essex East says seriously he would be practically crying. We would all need crying towels in this chamber.
That is the situation with regard to agriculture; it is critical.
As far as the hon. member is concerned, that is the situation with everything. The picture is as gloomy as it could be with everything; there is nothing right with anything.
Under this government.

So he admits it. In other words, his whole complaint is that he is no longer in a government, and I can understand that. If the present government were to offer the member for Essex East a place in the government overnight, his attitude would change completely and he would think that everything done by the government was just wonderful.
I assure you I would never go into a Conservative government.
Of course, we are talking about complete improbabilities and impossibilities here, but the hon. member recognizes, I think, that his gloom is purely political and is used for political purposes.
I would not agree with that. My sorrow is very genuine.
I know the hon. member's sorrow is genuine that he is not still a member of a government.
That is true.

The hon. member for Essex East said that the stabilization act has been of no benefit to Ontario wheat growers. This last year the price of Ontario wheat has been well above the support price because there was a short crop last year. That was because there was a great deal of winter killing and as a result of the short crop the price has been good. But the year before last this act was of very considerable benefit to the producers. It put them in the position where they could bargain with the buyers, and the powers that we extended to them under the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act enabled them to export at a subsidized price a certain amount of wheat to overseas markets and thus enabled the general price for Ontario winter wheat to be kept up to a reasonable level.
The hon. member for Essex East asked about an announcement concerning the sugar
[Mr. Harkness.)
beet support program. The representatives of the sugar beet growers have been down here this week, as a matter of fact, holding meetings with the stabilization board. The stabilization board has reported to me that the representatives of the growers went away quite happy as a result of these meetings. The discussion concerned particularly technical details as to how the support price was going to be applied in the three regions where it is applicable, and so forth, and I expect the stabilization board will in the very near future be making a recommendation to the government in regard to the level of support and the way in which they recommend it should be applied.
I might also say that, contrary to the hon. member's statement, the sugar beet growers last year were I think very well satisfied with the deficiency payments which they received from the government, and I have received quite a number of letters of appreciation and thanks from them on account of this payment.
The hon. member went on to say that my statement in regard to the dairy price support for the current year which I made on April 13 had misled the house and that butter scoring 40-93 represents only a small percentage of the butter produced; as a result, in some way the country had been misled.
I think there is no validity to this statement whatever. I stated quite definitely, as reported on page 3183 of Hansard for April 13 last, that:
The price support for butter during the dairy year May 1, 1960 to April 30, 1961 will be 64 cents per pound for Canada first grade creamery butter scoring 40-93, basis delivery Montreal, with appropriate price differentials for other grades and qualities.
The hon. member seems to take it for granted that we are paying 64 cents a pound for butter delivered to us which scores 4093, and a lesser price, which I said yesterday, I think, was 63 cents a pound, for butter scoring 39-92, and therefore that means we have reduced the price of butter, and so forth. I should like to point out, to begin with, that we only buy about one quarter of the butter produced in Canada and we sell most of that back again to the trade during the winter months. The great bulk of the butter produced in Canada goes directly into the trade. It does not trade at these prices but at varying prices at different times of the year. If hon. members look at the papers they will see it varies up and down from day to day. What these support prices do is to provide a floor at which we are prepared to buy the surplus packed in wooden boxes and so forth.

The actual situation is that the price of butter fat and the price of butter varies, as I say, up and down. It does not vary very much; it varies depending on the season of the year. I have the figures here for different seasons of the year and I can give as an example, churning cream. The prices paid to producers by plants in terms of cents per pound of butter fat varies, we find, from 65 cents in January at Edmonton to 63 cents, and it kept between those figures in Edmonton right through the year, varying between 63 and 65 cents. Then when we come to Winnipeg it varied from 60 to 66 cents. It varied between those two points throughout the year. I have the figures here for three years.
In London, Ontario, you have the same sort of thing. Hon. members will find that in London, Ontario the figure ranged from 65 cents to 68 cents throughout the year. In Three Rivers it varied from 67 cents to 72 cents at different times throughout the year. In other words, these are not absolutely fixed prices at which all the butter fat and churning cream sells. These are the prices at which we take over the surplus by purchase for resale from time to time later, which constitutes, in recent years, approximately one quarter, or a little less, of the production.
I might say further that the introduction of this distinction between 40-93 and 39-92 butter is something which many of the better dairymen have been asking for many years. This is the same kind of system as is in effect with regard to many other commodities; in other words, the customer pays a higher price for the better quality, and a lower price for a poorer quality. It puts the support of butter on a much sounder, more logical and more reasonable basis than has ever been the case before.
The hon. member for Kent (Ont.) spoke of the difficulty of securing farm labour. I think this is a difficult and increasing problem as far as farmers are concerned. It is one of the great anomalies in the so-called unemployment situation that such situations should arise. I know-because I was down in the hon. member's part of the country-that last year some of the sugar beets were not got up, despite the fact that in the city of Windsor in the constituency of the hon. member for Essex East there were thousands of unemployed. Nevertheless, the farmers could not get anyone to take up these beets.
I hope the minister is not suggesting that our workers are not prepared to work.

I am suggesting there is something seriously wrong with the unemployment figures when a situation of that kind
Supply-Agriculture
prevails, and a similar situation exists as far as agricultural work is concerned in all the areas of this country. You have farmers desperately trying to hire workers to take up their crops while at the same time there are cities not very far away which allegedly have thousands on the unemployment rolls. It is just not a situation that makes sense or which I can accept as being a true indication of what the unemployment situation is in this country.
The hon. member for Kent (Ont.) also spoke about the sales of agricultural products which have recently been made to Rumania and which were initiated and carried through to a considerable extent by Mr. Ernest Warwick of Blenheim, Ontario. I should like again publicly to express my thanks to Mr. Warwick for the extremely good work he did in this regard. I agree with the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) that we have to use improved methods as far as the sale of a number of farm products is concerned, because there is no doubt that most of them are in a surplus position throughout a large part of the world. These particular sales indicate that a certain amount of progress can be made along these lines if the right people are working on the problem.
That is the very question. The right people are not.

We have a lot of the right people and I expect we shall have more of them. Under the hon. gentleman's government, of course, no sales at all were made along these lines.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres spoke of the 25 cents per 100 pounds subsidy on milk for manufacturing purposes. He said confusion exists over this. There has never been any confusion whatever over this policy which was put into effect a little over a year ago. It has always been absolutely clear. It was discussed on its introduction and it has been discussed since on numerous occasions with all the national dairy organizations, and all those concerned with dairying are familiar with the situation. They know what it is. There is no confusion with regard to this matter whatever, and there should not have been any confusion as far as my statement is concerned.
Speaking on April 13-and I quote again from page 3183 of Hansard-I said:
-twenty five cents per 100 pounds will continue to be paid lor whole milk delivered for manufacturing purposes-
Then, later on, you will note this, Mr. Chairman:
-exclusive of milk from producers who sell a portion of their milk in the fluid, bottled milk
market.

Supply-Agriculture
I think that is as plain as English can make it. Anybody who sells a portion of his milk in the bottled, fluid market is not entitled to the 25 cents. That has been made absolutely clear, and there should have been no confusion at any time in connection with it.
The reason for that provision is, of course, that by and large the people who sell their milk in the fluid milk market-to the bottled trade-receive much higher prices than those who sell milk for manufacturing purposes. The idea of paying this 25 cents subsidy to those who sell milk for manufacturing purposes is in order to bring about to some extent an equality of price levels and to help to equalize the returns to the dairy farmer who sells to a cheese or butter factory.
The hon. member for Rosthem spoke about support prices. He suggested that support prices should be set at non-incentive levels. All I could say about that is that any attempt to fix a support price at a non-incentive level results in a price which is unacceptable to any farmer; no one is satisfied with it and, furthermore, it does not give any support. In order to have a support price which is effective, it is bound, by the very nature of things, to be an incentive price as far as a considerable number of producers are concerned and, particularly, as far as large integrated operations are concerned. If you set support prices and maintain support for a commodity by means of purchases at a price which is satisfactory to even a small proportion of bona fide farmers you will have provided in many cases-and I am thinking particularly of the poultry industry and the hog industry-a support price which is an incentive to large commercial integrated operations.
That is the very reason why this type of support price by means of purchase is not a practical means and not the best means of support as far as many commodities are concerned. The experience in the United States, particularly as far as wheat, cotton, corn and some other products are concerned, is a good example of the difficulties encountered if you attempt to maintain support by means of purchase. In the case of some commodities you can, but the method is not practical in the case of a large number of commodities; it is just not a practical or possible means of giving support to the bona fide farmer.
Might I ask just one question? Does that mean there is no intention to have a floor price on corn?
It does not mean anything of the kind. Corn has not entered into this discussion so far at all.
The minister just mentioned corn in the United States.

Yes, in the United States. But so far we have had no support prices for corn in Canada, as the hon. member knows. If we did have a support price for corn in Canada I am quite sure we would have to make it on a deficiency payment method of support the same as for soya beans.
The hon. member for Red Deer made a very useful and interesting speech particularly on farm credit, for which I would like to thank him. I know that he has been very intimately associated in the past with the granting of farm credit and his views on this subject are, I think, very valuable to the committee. I believe with him that through the Farm Credit Act it will be possible to greatly improve general agricultural conditions in Canada.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take up certain statements made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), with regard to the price of farm products, and more particularly dairy products, especially when he maintained that prices paid for dairy products in Canada were the highest in the world.
I do not wish to contradict the minister on that, but I must point out to him that the price of farm products means nothing if it is not established in proportion to production costs. When we speak of the sale price of some farm product, we naturally have to know how much it costs, and the minister made no reference to the production cost index.
I mentioned this in my remarks the other day, and I also said that production costs had gone up 16.9 points in the past year. If we compare the price of butter three or four years ago, and even six or seven years ago, and today, we will find that, at 64 cents a pound, the price of that produce today is not higher than when it was 58 cents three years ago. On the contrary, if we apply the same reasoning I just mentioned, butter should sell at 68 cents, in comparison to the 58 cents paid for it three years ago.
The hon. member for Joliette-TAssomp-tion-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) made some comparisons and asked questions about the price of butter. The minister told us what butter prices were in Edmonton, Winnipeg, London, and Three Rivers. For instance, he stated that in Edmonton, it was selling at 63 to 65 cents; in Three Rivers, 67 to 72 cents; and, if I understood him rightly, this was for the current year.
I have here an excerpt from the Gazette for May 3, that is, after the price change for

farm products was announced, and more particularly for butter. On the Montreal market, the price has fallen since the week of May 3. In the last weeks of March, butter was selling in Montreal at 64 to 66 cents a pound, whereas prices published in the Gazette for May 3 mentioned 63 cents and 65J cents. Therefore butter prices are down by 1 to 1J cents since the change in price of farm products was announced. Yet the minister claims that this change has no effect on farm prices.
That is what I wanted to point out for the information of members of the committee and of the Minister of Agriculture, because he does not seem to believe that this change in the price of butter will affect farmers income, since the government will surely buy the surplus production.
However, I have already stated, as did the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), that 70 per cent of butter production was graded 92. I fail to see how the minister can say that the prices of farm products will not be affected, when a reaction is already apparent on the Montreal market. And I do not doubt that the same thing will occur on other markets.
I should also like to say a few words about the price support policy on butter. The department now requires a producer to secure a registration certificate. That is a new method recently adopted by the department. Now, I am informed by some manufacturers that at the present time about one third of the farmers have not obtained their registration permit, which forces the manufacturer to pay an extra 25 cents per 100 pounds of butter delivered to him, because he does not want to lose his customers.
I am also informed that refunds are being made to the Department of Agriculture, and that these refunds are turned down because the formula is not filled in as the department would like it to be. I must point that if manufacturers are prepared to do this work free, it seems to me the department should consider this attitude on the part of manufacturers, and show better understanding when recommendations are made.
I am also informed that there are farmers today who have two or even three registration certificates. This is due to delay on the part, perhaps of manufacturers or of the department in providing permits to producers, which caused producers to file their request with the manufacturer of their choice, so that, finally, they were getting two permits.
What I am afraid of is that those permits
Supply-Agriculture
might be transferred to other farmers, as happened in the case of hog breeders. In fact questions were put on the orders of the day pointing out that some farmers often had two or three permits in their possession, in order to take advantage of deficiency payments on hogs. I am afraid that this will happen again with regard to dairy products.
The Minister of Agriculture also mentioned the 25 cents per hundredweight of milk delivered to manufacturers, who transformed it into butter, cheese and milk powder.
The minister claims that such a policy will not affect the farmers' income. Yet very many farmers in the province of Quebec are not in a position to sell all the fluid milk they produce.
They can sell one fifth of their production and the rest must be delivered to the butter, cheese and milk powder manufacturers. Therefore, the farmer cannot collect the subsidy of 25 cents per hundredweight.
Some farmers are losing $500 to $800 a year that way, and the average farmer is the one who takes the brunt of what I would describe as a segregationist policy.
Refusal of the 25 cents subsidy per hundredweight on milk delivered to a manufacture is contrary to the request made by the U.C.C., the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the farmers. The things requested are logical and, if granted, would do away with misrepresentation by some producers and avoid trouble to the department.
The minister has announced his policy. I do not think he will change his mind because each time we have made suggestions, he has not seen fit to give them favourable consideration.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to make after the speech of the Minister of Agriculture who, once again, disguises the truth by saying that the farmers' income for 1959 or 1960 will not be affected by his price policy on dairy products.
I would like to add a few words in reply to the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), who stated that, in the province of Quebec, there is a law against the sale of margarine. I will read a few lines from that act.
A section of that act does indeed prohibit the sale of margarine in the province of Quebec. We know, however, that some is being sold. The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm himself said in his remarks, that as much margarine as butter is being sold in the province of Quebec.

Supply-Agriculture
Section 6 reads as follows:
In the case of Infringement of a provision of this act or of a regulation made thereunder, any dairy product substitute which was the object of such infringement must be seized, with or without a warrant, as well as the container thereof and any vehicle used for its transportation, and the confiscation thereof shall be ordered by the court for the profit of the crown.
The penalty for such an infraction is set at $2. Section 5 reads as follows:
Whosoever infringes any provision of this act or of a regulation made thereunder shall be liable, if the offence relates to the possession, for other purposes than for sale, of a dairy product substitute, to a fine of not less than two dollars nor more than twenty dollars and costs, for the first offence, and to a fine of not less than five dollars nor more than twenty five dollars and costs, for each subsequent offence.
Oddly enough, however, the second paragraph of section 7 reads as follows:
Prosecutions for infringement of this act may be instituted by the crown or by any person previously authorized for such purpose by the Minister of Agriculture; in the latter case, the prosecutors shall be entitled to one half of the fine collected.
Mr. Chairman, this shows clearly that, in the province of Quebec there is an act prohibiting the sale of margarine or butter substitutes. But to prosecute people who sell margarine, permission must first be obtained from the minister of agriculture of the province of Quebec.
It is also known that in Quebec, a butter substitute called "spread" is sold by wholesalers, and inquiry shows that margarine sales in the province of Quebec are controlled by members of the Union Nationale government.
That is, Mr. Chairman, what I wanted to say to the hon. member for Joliette-l'Assomp-tion-Montcalm. If there is an act to this effect in the province of Quebec, it should be applied and the sale of butter substitutes should be prevented.

An unfounded charge.
(Text):

Is the minister not going to reply to some of the questions put to him, particularly as to the government's intention of an alternative program, such as acreage assistance? There is a story in today's paper-I am now looking for it- which indicates that the government intends to make an announcement very soon along those lines. If that is the case, can the minister not give us some indication today? If it is not the case, surely we are entitled, on the discussion of the agricultural estimates, to know if the government has any alternative

to the proposals made by western farmers over a year ago. It surely is not consistent with good government for the government continually to delay, now over a year, its answer to this request that concerns, not only farmers in all parts of western Canada but every member from western Canada who sits behind the government in this house.
Mr. Chairman, I think all I can say to the hon. member is that he should not believe everything he reads in the papers. He should have learned that by this time.
I find the press pretty reliable.

Certainly, what he has read in the paper I do not know anything about. What I would say on this question is that suggestions were made to the effect-I think it has appeared in a considerable number of papers-that the western farm organizations were asked to put in writing any alternative to deficiency payments which they wished to discuss with the Prime Minister and the cabinet, and we would then be very glad to have them come down and discuss the matter with us. Up to date they have not yet put in any alternative.

Does the minister think it is up to the farmers of this country to provide the solutions themselves? I do not know whether they feel the assistance plan is the way by which this problem could be solved. But is it not up to the government itself, in the face of an admitted situation, to provide some plan? It seems to me it is an abdication by this government of its responsibilities when it says to the farmers of western Canada, we will not do anything unless you write us and tell us what particular proposal you have in mind to discuss with us. If that is the position of the government, if that is the final position, as now stated by the Minister of Agriculture, then he has served notice on the farmers of western Canada that they cannot look to get from him and from this government an implementation of the promises which this government gave to them.

Mr. Chairman, as usual this is an example, of which we have had plenty from the hon. member, of many words meaning little or nothing. The farmers of western Canada and the farm organizations of western Canada I think know extremely well what the situation is. The farm organizations of western Canada had no hesitation, as a matter of fact, in coming down here with demands for deficiency payments. I do not think, when they can agree among themselves on any alternative plan, that they will

have any hesitation in coming down here to discuss it with us, but up to date I take it they have not done that.
Has the government no plan? That is the question. It is an admitted abdication by the government.

There is no such thing as any abdication or anything else along that line, Mr. Chairman. The government has all kinds of plans but, unlike the previous government, we are not trying to dictate to the farmers as to what plan they should accept, and so forth. We have asked them to bring down an alternative plan and we will be glad to discuss it with them, and we are waiting for them to do that.

Item agreed to.
2.	Information division including a grant in the amount of $26,000 to the agricultural institute of Canada, $638,410.
Carried.
Hon. gentlemen may steamroll, but these are tactics which will not be appreciated. We are a small group and we are going to fight for the rights of parliament.
There is an increase of $15,000 in this item; can the minister tell us what it is all about?

Mr. Chairman, I am not entirely clear as to what the hon. member means but I can give him some information as to the reason for the increase. As a matter of fact, as far as departmental administration is concerned, which includes the deputy minister, and some of the other chief administrative officers, he will note that the increase is $73,000. It is accounted for largely by increases in salaries, the normal increments that take place and so on. The total number of people in the administration branch has been increased by 10. Some of that increase is due to the transfer of personnel from other branches to the central administration branch in an effort to improve the general administration. That is the explanation of that particular item.

Item agreed to.
3.	Contributions to commonwealth agricultural bureaux in a total amount of £46,384, notwithstanding that payments may exceed or fall short of the equivalent in Canadian dollars, estimated as of December, 1959 which is, $123,516.
Would the minister explain the details of this vote and why there is this small decrease in the amount from last year?

Perhaps I had better explain that the commonwealth agricultural bureaux 79951-0-231
Supp ly-A griculture
are a group of organizations in British commonwealth countries operating under a central executive council of representatives of these countries which directs the activities of the bureaux. The main activity is the maintenance of an abstracting service. The commonwealth institute of biological control, which is located in Canada, collects and distributes information on parasites and destructive diseases. I think the hon. member wanted to know why there is a slight decrease. In past years there have been certain lapsing balances, in one year amounting to $2,900, in another year $12,000 and in another year $1,747. It is estimated that the cost this year will be about $2,000 less than last year. The real explanation is that there has been an effort to estimate a little more closely.

Item agreed to.
4.	Economics division, $751,838.
I see that the vote for the economics division for 1960-61 is $751,838 compared with $726,986 in the last fiscal year, and I note that 146 additional persons are covered-
No, not 146 additional but 146 all told.

There are 146 all
told or an increase of 10. I thank the minister for the correction. I am sure that these are well qualified individuals, but the purpose of employing anyone in the government service is so that they will study plans and make recommendations to the administration with regard to problems in all their aspects that exist in a particular field. I take it that in the economics division there must be individuals to whom have been assigned the task of studying the very problem which engaged the minister and myself a few moments ago namely what should be done to meet the demands of western agriculture. Is there any particular group in this division engaged in considering alternative plans or are we only to have alternative plans based upon suggestions by the farmers of western Canada themselves? The minister says he has no plans.
I did not say that.

The minister said, "The government is waiting for written proposals by the farmers themselves and we have not heard from the farmers". The only conclusion is that unless they hear from the western farmers there will be no policy announced by the government. I say that that is a most unusual statement for a minister to make. In the light of the fact that we are adding 10 persons to the economics division I ask the minister to tell us whether

Supp ly-A griculture
any of these individuals are addressing themselves to alternative proposals to meet the kind of problem which confronted the western farmers when they made the suggestion for deficiency payments? It is not good enough for the minister or the government to say, "We are waiting for a written reply from the farmers of western Canada". That is a most unusual statement and the more often I repeat it the more incensed I become with the fact that it is possible for the government of this country to be so weak in its attitude toward these problems as to bring about the inaction which now characterizes a government that was going to do so much for agriculture.
Well do I remember how the minister, when he sat over here, berated the former administration and how he would have become incensed if the minister of agriculture of that day had dared make the kind of reply which the minister made today. The minister says, "We are not going to do anything for agriculture in the west unless we get a written reply". It is like saying to someone applying for a job, "Send me a letter with your qualifications in writing and if I think they are worth while I will give the matter consideration".
Surely that is not what the Minister of Agriculture should say to the western farmers. He now has these new employees in the economics division. Are any of them going to be employed in providing the government with alternative solutions, solutions which the government now says it is waiting to receive in writing from the farmers of western Canada?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Essex East has given us another of these exhibitions of attempting to make black appear white to which we are becoming very accustomed in this chamber. I would say that what he is incensed about is that we have not, as the previous government to which he belonged would have done, attempted to ram something down the farmers' throats and thus provide a club for the hon. member and his colleagues to beat the government with. That is what he is incensed about.
As a matter of fact, the particular group of people we are now talking about are employed all the time in doing research work on general agricultural economic questions and on specific agricultural questions. One of them, for example, did a study of the tomato situation in British Columbia, and I referred to that when I was replying to the hon. member for Vancouver East the other day. They have done economic studies of practically all phases of agriculture from

the marketing point of view, from the production point of view and so on.
With respect to alternative schemes to assist the western farmers, a great deal of work has been done by myself and also by members of the economics branch in working out schemes of different kinds. The hon. member does not need to think for a moment that the government is deficient in schemes of assistance of various kinds which might or could be put into effect. I have had a considerable number of them worked out and different people in this branch have worked on the various implications of them, how they might affect different parts of the country and so on and so forth.

Item agreed to.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It being five o'clock, the house will now proceed to the consideration of private and public bills, the former having precedence, pursuant to section 3 of standing order 15.
The house in committee on Bill No. SD-42, for the relief of Brenda Mary Pardy Thacker -Mr. McCleave-Mr. Rea in the chair.

A week ago I suggested that if hon. members who have particular complaints with regard to some of these bills would mention the bill specifically by name it would be possible to deal with the non-contentious bills all together, as has been our practice in the past for a great number of years, and then get down to the particular ones on which they wish to speak. It seems to me that this course commends itself. I noticed the other day that we did not linger over the affairs of several insurance companies and pipe line companies but put those bills through in five minutes or ten minutes without very much debate. Perhaps we could allow that procedure to be an example for us this afternoon.

With respect to that particular suggestion, Mr. Chairman, may I make a comment or two? I realize that it is a bit out of order but perhaps if you will allow me a second or two and the committee will be generous enough to do that we could deal with this particular point raised by the hon. member for Halifax.
On Friday last a similar request was made and, as you will recall, I then raised other matters that had to be dealt with and that if we were to select those which were to be considered as difficult or ones which required

some discussion and agreed to pass the others en bloc and then proceed to the next item on the order paper, we would have to concern ourselves with what happened to the public bills in private hands and so on. Following that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River suggested that perhaps the hon. member for Halifax, before making such a request, should communicate with representatives from the other two parties in an effort to work out some amicable solution. As far as I am concerned, no such specific discussions were held. Until that occurs perhaps we might just as well proceed with the bills today at least as they appear on the order paper and in that order.

Mr. Chairman, there has been discussion. I think my hon. friend is getting a little bit afield when he makes a statement like that. I had discussion with him only a few moments ago, asking whether it would be possible to take that course; and I am asking now in the chamber whether it is not possible. If he says no, then we go ahead and do as we have been doing in the past.

I do not like to refer to private conversations but if the hon. member considers that to be consultation, I think he is under a misapprehension. He gave no evidence about how he came to know how they did not use the upstairs during the cold of winter or what the wood was put there for or when it was put there. He is not questioned about it. He volunteers the information very graciously and generously of his own volition. He was simply asked if there was one bedroom and he only had to answer yes or no as the case might be but he went on and pointed out that they did not use the upstairs during the cold of winter.
I think one is entitled to assume from this that Mr. Etheridge is either not disclosing the full content of the discussion he had that morning with the respondent and corespondent or he knew and had had some discussions with the people who lived in the house or had been in the house himself. Possibly in his part-time work he was hired as a carpenter to board it up for the winter so that it could not be used during that period. These are assumptions. I do not think the last one could be the case because he is fairly well taken up with his work in these cases. That was more or less a facetious comment, but apart from that how did he know that the respondent and corespondent, living together as man and wife, did not use the upstairs during the cold of winter. I think we are entitled to assume that somebody told him that, that there was some prior discussion with the respondent who had lived in the house since May of 1957 and had been there during the winter of 1957-58 and again during the winter of 1958-59. I think we can assume that some discussion took place.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Would he mind explaining what point he is making at the present moment?

I am making the point that the upstairs was boarded up and Mr. Etheridge knew about it beforehand and had had some discussions with these people. He had undoubtedly been there and made arrangements beforehand. There is another case which supports that view. Just after the June in January or June in February mix-up Mr. Etheridge had this to say, which shows either careful planning beforehand or pure coincidence:
-at 1.15 in the morning I drove up to where Mr.-was living at-on my way home-
Just coincidently he happens to be driving by on his way home at 1.15 in the morning. He then says that later at 7.15 that morning he met Mr. Brault on the particular street in question. One would assume that he had not staked out the place as private eyes are prone to do and watched it day after day. One would assume that in this instance he knew what was going to occur. One would assume that he also knew about the upstairs being closed off in the wintertime. If we are going to accept the fact that there is a common law arrangement, and that is what the Senate has done, then I think we should not clutter it up with evidence of this nature to try to prove that very vague point about adultery. I am sure that what has happened in this case is that some discussions have taken place. I am sure that Mr. Etheridge knew beforehand about the closing off of the upstairs to keep the cold out in the winter or the hot air downstairs because there had been prior discussions, and the reason there were prior discussions was that Mr. Etheridge, being familiar with the process of parliament granting a divorce and knowing from past experience what he would have to prove before parliament, made this arrangement-
